### Heisenberg's Uncertainty Principle
It is impossible to simultaneously determine both the exact position ($x$) and momentum ($p$) of a quantum particle. Mathematically:
$$\Delta x \cdot \Delta p \ge \frac{\hbar}{2}$$

### Non-Existence of Electrons Inside the Nucleus

Assume an electron resides inside a nucleus of radius $R \approx 10^{-14} \text{ m}$.
1. **Uncertainty in Position:** $\Delta x \approx 2R \approx 2 \times 10^{-14} \text{ m}$.
2. **Minimum Uncertainty in Momentum:** 
   $$\Delta p \ge \frac{\hbar}{2\Delta x} \approx \frac{1.054 \times 10^{-34}}{2 \times 2 \times 10^{-14}} \approx 2.63 \times 10^{-21} \text{ kg m/s}$$
3. **Corresponding Minimum Momentum:** $p \approx \Delta p = 2.63 \times 10^{-21} \text{ kg m/s}$.
4. **Calculated Energy of Electron:** Since $p \gg mc$ ($m = 9.1 \times 10^{-31} \text{ kg}$), we use the relativistic energy formula $E \approx pc$:
   $$E \approx (2.63 \times 10^{-21}) \times (3 \times 10^8) \approx 7.89 \times 10^{-13} \text{ J} \approx 4.9\text{ MeV}$$

**Conclusion:** Beta decay experiments show that nuclear electrons/beta particles possess only $2 - 3 \text{ MeV}$ of energy. Since an electron would require $\approx 20\text{ MeV}$ to be confined in a nucleus, electrons cannot reside inside the nucleus.
proTip: Use the relativistic approximation $E \approx pc$ because non-relativistic formulas yield unrealistically low energies for electrons confined to nuclear dimensions.
